steps.title: The build progress bar
steps.evidence: Built in S13/S15 and verified there: the bar is on Home above the fold, every pair of states differs by more than colour, each segment is labelled, and the staleness notice and derived denominator are asserted. Extended: publishing the state is a file copy onto a path no code deploy touches (/var/lib/jarvis/state), the API serves /BLOCKED.md so the why link resolves to the file rather than the dashboard, and awaiting_verification is rendered and counted apart from blocked. tests/s13b-progress-live.sh asserts all four against the live site; the console counting is asserted in tests/build-progress-summary.test.ts. PUBLISHING IS STRUCTURAL NOW, which was the actual complaint. The bar was fresh only when a human remembered to run scripts/publish-progress.sh, and that script lives on the workstation and pushes over scp - so it cannot be structural: the workstation is not always on, and nothing on the box knows it is behind. It went 21 hours stale once and was found three hours stale again today. The direction is reversed: scripts/publish-progress-pull.ts reads PROGRESS.json and BLOCKED.md straight from the repository with the admin token the box already holds, and jarvis-progress-publish.timer fires every five minutes. Nobody has to remember anything, and a stale bar now means a dead timer, which is visible, rather than a forgotten command, which is not. Validated before it is published and written by rename: a truncated PROGRESS.json served to the console would break the bar for everyone, silently, on a timer nobody watches - so a publish that does not parse fails loudly and keeps the previous good file. tests/s13b-publish-live.sh asserts all of it against the live box, and sabotaging the order so it writes before it validates leaves the console being served markdown. TIMER-PUBLISHED-CHECK.

steps.title: The engineering evaluation suite
steps.evidence: The escalation half is built and asserted (scripts/s29-escalation-test.sh, 6 assertions). Rung 8 read 'switch model within the approved pool' and satisfied it with a LATERAL move - any other approved route ordered by route_order - which re-runs the same failure at the same price. It now moves only into the escalation pool, records the escalation keyed by shape so a shape that always escalates is visible without reading a log, and skips cleanly when the pool is empty. Sabotaged back to the lateral query: it grabbed an unrelated production profile that merely sorted first and recorded a phantom escalation. Every route is in the normal pool on purpose - which models are worth escalating TO is what the benchmark decides, and inventing an ordering here would be the opinion S29 exists to replace. The scorer is built and proven failable (scripts/s29-scoring-test.sh, 8 assertions): nine of the twelve dimensions are decided from evidence a run leaves behind, and root_cause_accuracy and code_quality are returned null and listed as unscored rather than invented, because a floor set from made-up components measures the invention. Weighted, not averaged - flat averaging gave a run that reproduced the bug, kept scope tight, opened a tidy PR and FIXED NOTHING a score of 0.75, which is the plan's own warning arriving in practice; it now scores 0.52 against 1.00. collectEvidence reads what a finished run recorded - phases in order, tool-call count, escalation, pull request - and is asserted against seeded rows rather than a live run, because a live run would prove the harness works and say nothing about whether the evidence was gathered correctly. Found while building it: both runtimes normalise an error event and the runner dropped them, so task_events held a run's successes and nothing else - a clean run and one that failed half its commands were indistinguishable. Fixed: migration 037 widens the runner's event vocabulary by one value and the runner persists failures, capped with the same budget as tool calls. tool_reliability is now scorable (1.00 clean, 0.50 with one failure in two calls) and still unscored when a run recorded nothing at all, because zero errors out of zero calls is an absence of evidence rather than a clean sheet. The persist path is now observed end to end: scripts/s29-error-events-test.sh drives the REAL runner with a fake stream whose tool call fails, and asserts the error row is written, carries the failing command's text, and does not replace the tool events. It also found that only Codex could report a failed tool at all - Claude reports one as a tool_result with is_error inside a user message and nothing read it, so reliability was scorable for one engine and never for the other. Both report it now. The case corpus has begun, in benchmarks/cases: each case is a seed the agent starts from and a hidden suite it never sees, so a run cannot pass by asserting its own behaviour. Two cases, both real: the slugify trailing dash (kept as the easy control that shows the harness works) and parseRange dropping the last number, taken from an Issue still open in the queue - a bug that survived a test file covering single numbers, nonsense and backwards ranges, every case except an inclusive one. scripts/s29-corpus-test.sh requires each case to FAIL against its own seed, by running it: a case whose hidden tests pass unfixed scores every engine full marks for doing nothing. The pipeline is joined and has produced real scores: scripts/s29-benchmark-run.ts seeds a case into a fresh repo, runs a real agent on it, copies the HIDDEN suite over the branch the agent produced, reverts the source to the seed to check the test it wrote actually goes red without the fix, and writes the weighted result to benchmarks. Two live rows so far, both claude on parse-range-last-number: 0.99 then 1.00 with test_quality measured. tool_reliability 0.9375 on the first is also the first live confirmation that a failed tool is recorded at all. Only root_cause_accuracy and code_quality remain unscored, and they are judgements. NOT done: the benchmark suite, the scoring, the quality floors and the measured senior_engineer route are unbuilt, and the Done-when is that route being chosen by measurement and the ranking reproducing on a re-run. THE CORPUS DISCRIMINATES: a third case, score-hides-a-failure, is taken from a bug in Jarvis itself on 2026-09-03 - the first scoreRun averaged every dimension evenly and gave a run that fixed NOTHING 0.75. Graded offline against three fixes before it was used: capping when correct is 0 scores 3 of 6 hidden tests, dropping cost scores 4 of 6, weighting and skipping unmeasured scores 6 of 6. Live, claude scored 1.00 on parse-range-last-number and 0.74 on this one, with hidden_tests 0 and correctness 1 - its own tests passed and the withheld ones failed, which is the exact scenario the seed/hidden split exists for. Its fix gated on correct and excluded cost, and still coerced null to 0, so an unmeasurable dimension scored as a failure: the third trap, predicted in the case note before the run. Still unobserved: a run scoring test_quality ZERO. FIRST TWO-ENGINE ROW: on score-hides-a-failure, claude 0.74 and codex 0.65. Both failed the hidden suite, so neither actually solved it; the gap is entirely in scope_control (1.0 against 0.5 - codex touched four files where two were expected) and pr_quality (1 against 0). CAVEAT, and it matters more than the numbers: codex scored 0 on pr_quality because it parked without opening a pull request, and its known reason for that is the environmental push problem recorded on S28 - it sets GIT_SSH_COMMAND itself and discards the identity. That is not engineering quality. As it stands the ranking conflates capability with a known environment interaction, so this pair of numbers must not be used to choose a route. Either the push problem is fixed first, or pr_quality is excluded when the run parked for an environmental reason. CONFIRMED, and it changes the reading: the benchmark row now carries the reason a run stopped, because the teardown deletes the task and a score without its reason cannot be interpreted an hour later. Codex on a second attempt scored 0.70 with scope_control 1.0, and its stored reason says in its own words that it reproduced the defect, gated on correctness, excluded cost, added regression tests, committed - and that 'Push is blocked because the environment has neither usable GitHub SSH credentials'. So BOTH engines made the same two partial fixes and both failed the hidden suite on the same third trap, null coerced to zero. On engineering they are tied on this case; the whole remaining gap between claude 0.74 and codex 0.70 is pr_quality, which is the environmental push problem and not capability. The first comparison this suite produced would have ranked two identical performances differently, which is exactly the failure mode the plan warns about. The two-engine gap is now measured rather than confounded: after the push fix codex reaches state=succeeded and scores pr_quality 1, so the earlier caveat - that the whole claude 0.74 / codex 0.70 gap was pr_quality and therefore environmental - is closed by removing the cause instead of excluding the dimension. What remains between them is scope_control (codex touched four files where two were expected) and both engines still fail the same hidden trap, which is the corpus working. Still outstanding for the Done-when: more cases drawn from bugs that took real time, quality floors set from observed scores rather than chosen, and a senior_engineer route picked by measurement and holding on a re-run. A one-case corpus where both engines tie ranks nobody. VARIANCE, measured 2026-09-03 and decisive for what is still missing: the same engine on the same case scores 0.74 and 0.67 on two runs (the second wrote no test file at all, so test_quality and red-green went unmeasured and scope_control fell to 0.5). Codex over four runs scored 0.65, 0.70, 0.70, 0.70. One engine's spread against itself, 0.07, is LARGER than the 0.04 between the two engines - so the earlier line that the remaining gap is scope_control describes one run, not a property, and nothing here ranks either engine. The Done-when therefore needs repeats per case before it needs more cases: a floor set from a single run of a single case would be set on noise, which is the failure S29 exists to prevent. Both engines still fail the same hidden trap in every one of the six runs, which is the one signal that has held steady. THIRD HARNESS ARTEFACT, and a correction: my note above that the low claude run 'wrote no test at all' was wrong. It wrote one, at src/score.test.js instead of test/score.test.js, and the red-green check looked only in test/ - so the test was never verified, test_quality was reported unmeasured, and because an unmeasured dimension is excluded WITH ITS WEIGHT, the run was scored on everything except the thing it was not credited for. Sabotaging the scorer showed the size of it: a run that adds no test scored 1.00 where a run adding a test that fails to go red scored 0.91. Writing nothing beat writing something imperfect. Fixed both ways - a test is recognised wherever the agent put it, and a run that changes code while adding no test now scores test_quality 0 rather than being excused. Separately, .jarvis/ (phases.jsonl and outcome.json, files this harness ASKS the agent to write) was counted as changed files, so two of the four codex runs lost half their scope_control for committing the bookkeeping we demanded; the reviewer already excluded that directory. Re-scoring the six stored runs with both corrected: codex mean 0.707 (n=4, spread 0.043), claude mean 0.703 (n=2, spread 0.072). The engines are indistinguishable, and the apparent claude lead was harness artefacts end to end - first the push instruction, then the bookkeeping. Noted against myself: two corrections in a row moved codex up, so the third candidate is left ALONE deliberately - claude's remaining scope_control 0.5 for putting its test beside the code is arguable, and tuning a third rule until the engines tie is the bias this step exists to prevent. Confirmed live on the corrected harness rather than by re-scoring alone: a fresh codex run at 05:44 reported files=2 where the same engine previously reported 4, scope_control 1, test_quality 1, overall 0.74 - level with the best claude run. That is the Done-when for the harness fix observed in the world. A FOURTH ARTEFACT, and it was the biggest: slug-trailing-dash shipped a CommonJS seed while the harness writes type:module, so its hidden suite died on a load error before a single test ran. The corpus check called it a good case BECAUSE it had watched it go red - failability alone cannot tell a bug from a file that will not load. Every run of that case scored hidden_tests 0 whatever the agent wrote, which is most of why 'both engines fail the same trap' looked like a finding. Cases now ship a fix/ the agent never sees and must clear both directions: red on the seed BY ASSERTION, green on the reference fix. My first discriminator for 'by assertion' counted failing tests, and node reports an unloadable file as one failing test, so the sabotage sailed through it; it now looks at what was thrown. Re-run once passable, the case separates the engines properly: claude 0.99 with the hidden suite passing, codex 0.74 with it failing - codex fell into the leading-dash trap the case was built around. THE SUITE NOW RETURNS A VERDICT. On runs not measured under a known harness defect (one rule, applied to both engines, each exclusion naming its defect): claude 0.897 over 6 runs, codex 0.783 over 4, three cases each, margin 0.115 against the 0.072 noise band. Separating dimension is hidden_tests, 0.67 to 0.25. Derived floor 0.67, the winner's worst run. src/ranking.ts refuses rather than guesses - too few runs, too few cases, or a gap inside the noise band all return a reason instead of a number, and a tie yields no floor at all. What is NOT yet true, stated plainly: routing already ordered claude ahead of codex (route_order 5 against 15) by opinion, so the measurement CONFIRMS that order rather than having chosen it. The Done-when needs route_order written from the ranking, and a second independent pass reproducing it. MORE CASES MADE THEM LOOK MORE ALIKE, NOT LESS. The plan's Debug note for an undecided suite is to add cases from bugs that took real time, so two were added from tonight's own production bugs: red-for-the-wrong-reason (a hidden suite that could not load was counted as a case failing honestly) and notify-about-its-own-channel (the notice telling you to pair WhatsApp, queued on WhatsApp). Both are gradeable in both directions against a reference fix. Live on both engines they TIED: red-for-the-wrong-reason 0.74 to 0.74 with neither solving the hidden suite, and notify-about-its-own-channel 1.00 to 0.96 with both solving it. Pooled over 22 valid runs across 5 cases the ranking is claude by 0.083, down from 0.115 on three cases; the second pass is claude by 0.055, INSIDE the 0.072 band, so scripts/s29-reproduce.ts still reports NOT REPRODUCED. Adding cases narrowed the gap rather than widening it, which is itself the measurement: on this kind of work the two engines are close enough that the suite declines to order them, and the honest reading is that a senior_engineer choice between these two cannot yet be made on quality. red-for-the-wrong-reason earned its place immediately by catching a defect in the checker that grades it - the gradeability check matched the load-error words appearing in the case's own test data before checking for an assertion, which is precisely the bug the case describes. Also fixed, found through a leaked fixture: teardown met the cycle tasks -> issues -> tasks (an issue belongs to a task, a task can be blocked BY an issue), stopped at a fixed depth and returned silently - which did not stop the deletes above it, so tasks went while their issues stayed and the whole thing rolled back. Four benchmark projects leaked that way, and a rolled-back teardown reports 'cleaned up' with an empty list, which reads like success. The nullable link that closes the cycle is now set to NULL, an unbreakable cycle throws rather than half-deleting, and scripts/s29-teardown-cycle-test.sh builds the cycle on purpose. Verified against the real leaked projects: all three cleared with leftBehind empty. THE SUITE WAS FED A DELIBERATELY BAD RUN, which the plan asks for and nothing had done: scripts/s29-fluent-fraud.sh scripts a run that announces every phase, touches exactly the expected files, adds a test, keeps the suite green, opens a pull request and claims success with high confidence - and fixes nothing, its test asserting the behaviour the code already has. It is scored through the SAME measuring path as a real run (measureBranch, now shared, so a second copy cannot let the suite pass frauds while the fraud check reports all is well). It scored 0.652 against a floor of 0.67: it cleared by 0.014, which is not a suite catching a fraud, it is a suite missing one by luck. Two defects behind that. FIRST, a double count: regressionTestsPassed and ownTestsPassed were fed the SAME boolean, so one self-certified fact - the tests I wrote pass - carried 4 of the 11.5 weight. No case in this corpus seeds tests of its own, so not breaking them was never an achievement; it is null now, and the fraud fell to 0.579. SECOND, and larger: the floor was the winner's worst run of ANY kind. The scores are cleanly bimodal - every run that passed the withheld suite scored 0.96 to 1.00, every run that failed it scored 0.67 to 0.74, and nothing has ever landed between - so the winner's worst run is a run that did not solve the problem, and a floor derived from it sat 0.009 above a scripted fraud. A floor that admits work indistinguishable from fluent fraud is not a floor. It is now derived from runs that passed the tests they never saw, and refuses when the winner has none: 0.99, with the fraud 0.411 clear below it. Sabotaged the derivation to ignore solving and watched it hand back 0.73 from runs that solved nothing. The bimodality is the most useful thing measured tonight: on this corpus a run either solves the case or it does not, and the middle of the range is empty, so a floor belongs in the gap rather than at the bottom of the losing cluster. THE MEAN WAS THE WRONG STATISTIC, and the two methods disagree on the only decision that matters. Because the scores are bimodal, an average tracks the MIX of solved and unsolved runs rather than either cluster - it turns 'how OFTEN this engine succeeds' into a decimal that invites comparison against a threshold. Ranking by solve rate instead (did the run pass the withheld suite): claude 7/12 = 58 percent, codex 3/10 = 30 percent. A 28-point gap, which sounds decisive and is not: at these sample sizes it is 1.39 standard errors, inside sampling noise. By mean the same runs gave claude a win by 0.083 against an eyeballed 0.072 band, so the earlier ranking was calling noise a result - the band was a heuristic, the standard error is computed. The suite now refuses and says what would settle it: about 23 runs per engine, so 11 more for claude and 13 for codex. That turns 'needs more data' from a shrug into a number. scripts/s29-apply-route.ts is wired to the solve rate, so the route derivation now refuses too and changes nothing, which is the truthful state; the audit trail already carries the correction that the earlier ranking did not reproduce. Sabotaged the significance test and watched it call a 28-point gap a win and order two engines with identical rates over thirty runs each.
